title: Crime and Punishment, Dostoyevsky
subject: litterature
description: In 1866, Raskolnikov killed a loan shark to prove that he was a superman. Dostoyevsky transforms this crime into a laboratory of conscience and redemption.

hero.hook: A murder committed for a theory. And an unforgiving conscience.

blocks.text: Published in **1866**,  is one of the greatest novels by **Fyodor Dostoyevsky**. **Rodion Raskolnikov**, poor student from **St. Petersburg**, commits a double murder while believing he is defending an abstract idea. Much more than a psychological thriller, the book explores guilt, **nihilism** and the possibility of spiritual rebirth. **[[Crime and Punishment]]**

Dostoyevsky does not just recount a crime. He makes it a laboratory where an intellectual theory brutally clashes with the reality of human consciousness. The novel asks a question that remains burning: can we kill in the name of a superior idea?

sections.title: The author facing the abyss: biography and context

blocks.text: Dostoyevsky wrote this novel riddled with debt, under pressure from his publisher. In **1849**, member of , he suffered a mock shooting on **Semenovski** square, then left for  in Siberia for four years of forced labor. This confrontation with death profoundly transforms his vision of the world. **[[Petrashevsky Circle]]** **[[Omsk penal colony]]**

blocks.caption: Fyodor Dostoyevsky, novelist of conscience and suffering.

blocks.text: Dostoyevsky burned a first manuscript in the first person before starting again in the third person to gain narrative distance.

Returning from exile, he fought the **[[Russian nihilism of the 1860s]]**, an intellectual movement which rejected all moral and religious authority in the name of reason and science. **Crime and Punishment** shows how an idea cut off from concrete life and love can lead to crime. Raskolnikov is not a monster: he is a brilliant intellectual who considers himself a superman.

sections.title: The temptation of the superman: Raskolnikov's theory

blocks.text: Raskolnikov divides humanity into "ordinary" and "extraordinary". The latter, like **Napoleon**, would have the right to transgress the moral law for a higher goal. To test his theory, he kills an old loan shark who he considers useless and harmful to society, with an ax he borrowed from the concierge.

blocks.caption: 19th century Saint Petersburg: poverty and intellectual fever.

blocks.text: The crime goes wrong: he also kills **Lizaveta**, the old woman's innocent sister, who overhears the murder. He does not profit from the stolen money, which he hides under a rock. Raskolnikov discovers that he is not the superman he thought: his conscience cannot stand blood, and fever consumes him.

The “punishment” begins with the murder, well before the court. Raskolnikov isolates himself, unable to bear the contact of his mother **Poulcheria** or his sister **Dounia**. Judge **Porfiry Petrovich**, master of , knows he is guilty but lets him accuse himself. **[[Forensic psychology]]**

In front of him emerges **Sonya Marmeladova**, a young woman sacrificed to prostitution to feed her family. She reads the **[[Resurrection of Lazarus]]** episode and opens a non-rational path: confession and love. Where Raskolnikov raised himself through intellectual pride, she lowered herself through love of others.

sections.title: The Resurrection and Inheritance of a Total Work

blocks.text: The epilogue in Siberia shows a slow and difficult . Raskolnikov does not immediately abandon his theory of the superman, but Sonia's love gradually pierces his intellectual shell. **Nietzsche** would later recognize Dostoyevsky as an exceptional psychologist of guilt and transgression. **[[Redemption through suffering]]**

The novel remains hot today: can we kill in the name of an abstract idea, of a “great cause”? Dostoyevsky responds that human conscience always ends up claiming its due, and that true rebirth comes through humiliation and love, not through reason alone.
**Crime and Punishment** shows the failure of intellectual pride in the face of moral reality. Raskolnikov's real punishment is not prison, it is isolation of the soul.
